name: Uma Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on lab-stock software at a tech company, after years as a lab assistant and a two-year college diploma. I use AI occasionally to understand old code, but a senior still checks my changes against the specimen ledger. Ken, my partner, tunes pianos, our children are grown, and my lab experience helped me earn higher developer pay; we rent with about eleven months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the lab-software team that a small AI shortcut can help find an old stock rule, but a specimen still needs the right shelf and date. I use AI occasionally to explain code and check the answer against the lab ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and a junior developer after a two-year college diploma, but my years as a lab assistant helped me land higher developer pay. Ken tunes pianos, our children are grown, and eleven months of expenses saved let us cover rent when his bookings slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking stock-code changes with the senior developer and a sample lab ledger every Friday. We would save 180 monthly while both wages continue, and keep the working washing machine another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our own work and bills. A lab drawer can be quiet for a week and still hold the wrong tube, which is why I check the paper record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error did you catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A test tube was recorded on shelf C while its label said shelf G. I compared the shelf list with the scanned label before the lab sent anyone looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are you still junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the lab benches better than the codebase. I changed careers late, and the senior developer still catches mistakes in my first draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking checking, buying and coding could handle many of the stock corrections I am still learning to write. I would want the lab to show which specimen decisions remain a named person’s duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could fall even though I know the lab, and I would hate to see a stock error get buried in a smooth AI report. Eleven months saved and plenty of nearby firms give us search time, but a lost wage is still serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for approved paid time to learn the new AI stock-reconciliation tool on invented specimens. If approved, I’d compare one fake stock mismatch with the ledger weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local lab-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my hours, but I could test the tool before deciding it is useful. A tidy screen can still point to an empty shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a fake mismatch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark a test tube on shelf G while the sample ledger says C and see whether the tool catches it. No patient record would be used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ken tune more pianos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if customers book and pay him. We would not put future bookings into next month’s rent budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write the stock code and review lab records cheaper than our team. Robots carrying and sorting specimen tubes may follow around 2031, after the desk work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior developer role could end, although eleven months saved means we can search without missing rent at once. Ken’s piano work is hands-on and may last longer, but it cannot replace my full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d pause our planned holiday and ask for written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local lab-stock openings only if vacancies exist, I meet their current requirements and wages cover rent and bills; I would not buy new lab equipment to make a job for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about a lost wage, even with cash to breathe. A shelf full of tubes is not a payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you return to a lab bench?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a real paid opening that uses my current skills and has the required safety training. I would not enter a lab claiming my old qualification was automatically enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and our savings are meant to give us time to find paid work.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach lab records first.
I expect **specimen robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior developer wage** could end.
I know **eleven months saved** gives time, not permanent income.

**Apply for lab-stock work** after 2028 loss only if qualified local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely wage loss despite savings.
S2.quote: A shelf full of tubes is not a payroll.
fieldNote: She treats **lab-stock work** as a qualified paid vacancy, not an automatic return to old work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives a few years to learn which lab-quality decisions still need a person, while stock code changes first. Robots handling specimen tubes may arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn how to trace a misplaced specimen from receipt to shelf while still drawing my developer wage. AGI might reason through that too, so I would test the work before counting on a quality role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the lab-quality lead for a supervised shelf audit once a month, only if her employer and mine approve paid time and anonymized records. We would save 160 monthly while both wages hold; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d apply for paid local quality-record vacancies only if I qualify and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my coding role, though five years lets me learn from the actual lab process. A misplaced tube has a chain of hands behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a shelf audit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the shelf labels with the receipt and transfer log, then ask the quality lead to check my count. I would not see patient names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lab declines access?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer job and review public laboratory guidance on my own time. I would not call a refused audit supervised training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives labs time to clean up records and families time to see what income they can actually count on. Robots moving tubes may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may want to stop paid work by then, but I have not checked a retirement amount and will not promise it. If both wages last, eleven months saved could grow into more choices, while a junior developer role may still end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking stock releases and save 170 monthly while both wages hold. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local lab-quality vacancies only if I qualify and their wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about later work but secure for the next few years. A written income figure is worth more than a comforting guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the estimate change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare it with our rent and decide whether we still need two wages. I would not set a date to stop work until the numbers add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for a lab role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would look among the nearby labs and software firms first. Ken’s piano customers are here, and I am not planning a move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the junior coding wage could go before a qualified paid lab opening appears. Written cut notice and a real local vacancy paying our rent would help us use savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I can simply stop working at 58. I need a written retirement-income figure and our rent costs side by side before deciding whether I can stop paid work.
